comments.text: The choice of medical school matters less than the high cost of becoming a physician. While scholarships exist, medical education often requires substantial borrowing and should be viewed as a major investment. If admissions processes favor only wealthy applicants, medical schools risk admitting students who may be less prepared or less willing to care for patients across all socioeconomic backgrounds. That is not a sustainable approach. The larger barriers are the pressures physicians face every day: insurance companies controlling what care is approved, declining reimbursement for services, rising professional liability costs, patient's unrealistic expecations, growing government data-reporting requirements, less time with patients, increased documentation demands, higher patient quotas, complex billing and coding expectations, and little support for work-life balance. These are just some of the factors contributing to physician burnout and driving doctors to leave medicine.
